cim: Are We Subjects or Objects? Bosnia, the Bosniaks, Zionism and Artificial Intelligence
cim_eredeti: Are We Subjects or Objects? Bosnia, the Bosniaks, Zionism and Artificial Intelligence
szoveg_eredeti:
Enver Rizvo share concerns regarding narratives of Bosniak scientific need and dependence. He argues that there is an urgent need to question narratives tying scientific progress to pro-Israel business and political policy. These narratives obscure the urgent need for oversight and discussion of AI projects aligned to Zionist figures and projects. Such oversight, he argues, is vital for the ecological and political reasons as well as the ethical culture and identity of Bosnia.

On October 19th 2026, Prof. Dr. Nusret Isanović appeared as a guest on Oštristav, a podcast episode produced by the Bosnian-Herzegovinian media outlet STAV. According to the description accompanying the podcast, Isanović discussed the profound moral crisis and the abuse of religion, the misconceptions of contemporary society, geopolitical tensions, and the dangers posed by artificial intelligence (AI) in the hands of magnates. He reportedly warned against the illusions in which we live, while also offering a key to raising awareness through upbringing, education and culture. Nothing would have been problematic about this matter, had Isanović himself not, at one point during the podcast, succumbed to certain illusions, those in which he believes, perhaps wishes to believe, or wishes to persuade broader segments of the Bosniak population to accept.

What, precisely, is the matter? In one segment of the podcast, which was separately extracted from the full episode and published on STAV’s official Instagram account, presumably to ensure that its message reached the widest possible audience, Isanović expressed a whole series of highly problematic VIEWS. In this excerpt, Nusret Isanović states:

“Could we, for example, have had fifty PhDs in artificial intelligence by now? The Serbs recognized this. Do you know that the Serbs have hundreds of their best and most talented people pursuing master’s degrees, doctorates and postdoctoral studies in Israel? Because Israel is a country where the most significant expertise in fields such as nanotechnology and artificial intelligence is concentrated. Almost everything that exists in Silicon Valley can also be found in Israel, perhaps even in a more relevant sense. And people have recognised this. So, what I want to say is this: we are not subjects, you know. We have not been governing ourselves for quite some time. We do not make decide for ourselves.”

From Islamic Civilisation to the Israeli Model

In case there is any difficulty understanding Isanović’s message, it is worth reading it once again, if for no other reason than to recognize how he intends to raise awareness among broader segments of the Bosniak population. Isanović, namely, does not want the Bosniak people to fall behind the Serbs (a construct that is itself problematic, as it stems from a deeply problematic nationalist perspective), and calls for intensifying educational cooperation with the criminal Zionist entity of Israel. To understand the full implications of his position, however, we must first examine who Nusret Isanović actually is.

Nusret Isanović (born on October 25th 1954 in Gradačac) is a Bosnian-Herzegovinian philosopher, university professor and researcher of Islamic philosophy. He graduated in Philosophy and Sociology from the Faculty of Philosophy at the University of Sarajevo, obtained a Master’s degree in Philosophy, and earned his doctorate at the Faculty of Islamic Studies in Sarajevo. He previously served as dean of the Islamic Pedagogical Academy in Zenica and worked as a professor at the Faculty of Islamic Studies at the University of Sarajevo. His scientific research focuses on Islamic philosophy, culture, civilization and art.

It is particularly problematic, therefore, when someone professionally engaged in Islamic philosophy, culture and civilization, and active within the academic and religious institutions of the Bosniak society, ideologically aligns himself with Zionism, a political project whose historical realization and contemporary consequences stand in profound contradiction to the anti-colonial, emancipatory and humanist principles invoked by a significant part of the Islamic intellectual tradition- or, at the very least, ought to be invoked by it.

Nusret Isanović is not, however, the first among Bosniak intellectual to have gravitated towards a Zionist project that has, over the recent period, intensified its efforts to establish a presence in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Particular attention was drawn to an incident in April 2026, when Hikmet and Harun Karčić, founders of the Sarajevo Security Conference and sons of the late Prof. Dr. Fikret Karčić, a figure towards whom Bosniak Muslims feel a particular attachment, appeared in Mostar at an event hosted by Amir Gross Kabiri. The event was a promotion of the novel Itamar K. by Iddeo Netanyahu, the brother of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, organized by Kabiri, president of the M.T. Abraham Group.

Their appearance sparked public controversy, followed by the Karčić brothers’ denial of having attended the book promotion, claiming that they had entered the room by chance while waiting for a previously arranged business meeting with the management of Mostar’s Aluminij company. Thus, an encounter that raised a series of questions about social and institutional ties to Kabiri’s circle developed into a public controversy. The incident, however, was quickly forgotten and swept under the rug, while the Karčić brothers were effectively exonerated in the eyes of broader segments of the Bosniak public. Another section of the Bosniak academic elite came to their defense during those days, naturally interpreting the entire affair as an attempt at provocation or defamation, as Bosniak intellectual elites, constrained by their conformism, are unwilling, afraid perhaps, to see a larger picture.

Among those who defended them was Emir Suljagić, the current director of the Srebrenica Memorial Centre, who even argued that cooperation with Zionist circles was the only way to protect the status of the Srebrenica genocide, adding that, if forced to choose between Srebrenica and Gaza, he would choose Srebrenica.

Nevertheless, this is not merely a matter of isolated incidents, although it might appear so at first glance. What is at play is a serious symptom permeating Bosniak society and the public sphere, a symptom and a problem about which, as with so many other matters, there is not a lot that has been said. It is a phenomenon that could be described as the advance of Zionism into Bosnia’s public and social space, an advance for which Bosniak-Muslim intellectual elites are collectively, and through their networks, rolling out the red carpet. Let us therefore examine what this symptom reveals through Nusret Isanović himself. And since so many things in Bosnia and Herzegovina are frequently turned upside down, let us begin at the very end of the statement published in the Instagram video.

There, Isanović raises the question of Bosnia and Herzegovina’s political subjectivity, claiming that “we have not been governing ourselves for quite some time” and that “we do not make decide for ourselves”. The problem lies in such an uncritical acceptance of the proposition that we are not independent, because it effectively surrenders our capacity for decision-making, from the individual to the collective and state levels, to external centers of power. Independence does not mean the absolute absence of interdependence. Rather, it means the ability of individuals, societies and states to independently shape their own objectives, values and political decisions without having to subordinate them to the interests of others. When such dependence begins to be presented as an immutable historical fact, the very idea of political emancipation is lost, while responsibility for one’s own social and political processes is replaced by fatalism.
